projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Albert Pekrul was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Albert E. Pekrul. Mr. Pekrul served in the U.S. Army with the 212th Field Artillery. He served in the European Theater, and his highest rank was PFC. I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at Mr. Pekrul's home in Parma, Ohio, on February 14th of 2003. Al was 80 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: 1941. I was living with my dad on East 32nd Street in Cleveland, off of Payne Avenue, in 41. I just had gotten out of Three C Camp.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: Civilian Conversation Corp, in 41. And we'd moved from the west side to the east side where I met my wife 63 years ago. But, anyway, lived there till we got--we got married in 1942, and the year after we got married I--had a baby boy--on my 21st birthday got sworn in the Army in--Fort--Fort Hayes, Columbus, yeah. And on my 21st birthday sworn in the Army. Left my wife home with a little baby a month old. And I went from--.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when would that be? In 1943?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 42 is when you were sworn in? Okay.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: No 43 I got sworn in. I was married in 42.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were married in 42.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: Yeah. 43 I got sworn in the Army April 21st on my birthday. And from there I went to Camp Polk, Louisiana. I call it "Lousy-ana" always. Had basic training with some academy from Annapolis. Seventeen weeks of basic training, and it was tough. Infantry training, hybrid infantry, jumping out of half tracts, you know, attacking and going up a hill with the gunnery arms, crawling up the hill, rolling. The worst part of that whole deal was march up 25 miles out to a bivouac area, we were supposed to be attacked that night. I was the only guy with water in my canteen. I don't need much water to march. I mean, cause I was in pretty good shape. Got out there and just about a couple of miles before we got out there took a swig of water, guy says, you got water, you got water. Passed the canteen around, about five minutes it's all gone. Five minutes it was all gone. Had an empty canteen. Get in the bivouac area, had to dig in, pull guard. No attack came, but we were on alert. We got up early in the morning. Had breakfast. Marched back to camp. We were in the full field. Got back to camp at 3:15 in the afternoon. I remember the time, because I figured we were done for the day. Lieutenant said, got 15 minutes to put your stuff away, fall out for calisthenics. I went in and got my stuff up. I lay down on the floor. You couldn't lay on your bed. He said, don't lay down on your bed, cause, you know, they inspect the barracks. They said they would; they didn't though. Lay down on the floor. A whistle blew, we had to get up and get out. Had my body on the floor of the dang barracks soaking wet. Course, naturally your feet, I mean, blisters broke, broke, and re-broke, but It was tough training. We made it through it though. So had a squad, get in a squad. Went home on furlough for two weeks. Come back and was going to make the rank. Come back and they said our outfit was dissolved, broke up. I was going to artillery. Now, you had infantry training, right? You had ____ tanks, halftracks, Jeeps, everything. Every vehicle that was armored. Fired all the guns they had, all the guns. Imagine being on a range for eight hours firing machine guns, M1's, .50 calabur machine guns, then goes submachine guns into these silhouette targets, boom, boom, boom. I come to artillery, right, 212 Field Artillery Battalion, National Guard outfit. All these guys are my seniors, believe me. They're old. They're 35, maybe 40. I replaced a guy was 55; they don't want to take him overseas, right? Come in there, infantry man. Got to learn the artillery all over, the ____ hop and all that, the gun. So ranks were told. You didn't get a rank cause you're a rookie, right, in artillery. But you're infantry, so I show those guys how to strip field an M1 and all that. We were in--other than Camp Polk, Louisiana, come back and had to go to Camp Cook (ph), California to join the outfit. Going in there a rookie. Don't know nobody. I mean have to train with the infantry all those months, I mean, well, 17 weeks. Go in there, gee, that's a gun, the gun M7. What the hell's an M7 tank, you know. M7 tank is a tank that has no top on it. Has a gun that traverses 90 degrees. So if you get on a target you had to move--you have to move the tank, you have to move 90 degrees. Machine gun on top of the rig, so naturally infantry, machine gun. So we've on maneuvers and all that with machine guns, ____+ shells. So we're training over there in the desert. We think we're going over to the South Pacific. In about a month and a half's time I'd moved from Cleveland to Camp Polk to California. My wife wanted to join me in California. I said, you can't. I couldn't tell her why not. We come all the way from California back to New York. Being shipped out to Europe. I called my wife. I had a 24-hour pass. I'd come from Cleveland to California. I told her I'd meet her in New York, the USO in New York. I didn't know nothing about New York. But some of these guys were from New York. We'll show you, we'll show you. Okay. I met her in Grand Central Station. I don't know where the hell it was at. Spent a night in New York. Then I get up at 4:30 in the morning to get back to camp or be AWOL, because we're getting ready to pack to go overseas. I mean, I couldn't tell her nothing. So 24 hours I come back. I was whipped. I didn't know how she got home, because we got on the boat the same day. We were in the port getting ready to be shipped out. Was it Camp Shanks? Camp Shanks, I think. Getting ready to get shipped out. Okay, we go overseas. Eleven days on the boat. February. Up and down, up and down, sideways. Several of them got seasick. Had to pull their guard duty for them. Had to pull KP. Naturally you had to pull KP, naturally. But that wasn't bad, but teeing on a ship--. Were you ever on a ship?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: It was sea ship up and down, sideways. We're eating, you're standing up. You ain't sitting down. Stand up. You're swaying back and forth. The worst part of the whole deal was to have some guy across from you whee throw up--to throw up. Eleven days out we got a couple of submarines scares, but nothing happened there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get sick?

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: The first--when we were pulling out of port by the Statute of Liberty, that first little movement, we were playing cards. It wouldn't have bothered me until somebody said, we're moving, we're moving. So all of a sudden everybody got sick whether you're moving, but I wasn't sick, I just had a little dry heave more or less. After that I was okay. I mean it was surprising. I was okay after that. So dry land--. Sailors they got sick, we had to pull their guard for them. Those that got sick we had to pull guard duty for them. So 11 days on a boat in a hole. Once in a while go up to get fresh air. We were down three, three decks down below. Playing crap naturally, shooting crap. And the johns on the boat at that time--this is an old boat, the USS Roosevelt--had johns, the toilets, had water running back and forth, you know, in a tray-like, a trough, back and forth. Had to go to the john, that water going back and forth. I mean. It's funny now that you think of it. We slept in hammocks, the swaying, I mean, which was good, you slept good in them. We landed. There was one guy on our ship that was sick for the whole 11 days. He couldn't get out of bed or anything. The guys had to carry him to the john. I mean, he was really sick. We fed him juice, juice. We landed in Scotland in a little canal way in Scotland. And this guy, I mean, he looked at the ground, oh, he looked at the ground. He was pale. He lost--I don't know how many pounds he lost. He was really sick. Glasgow, Scotland. We had to help him down the gangway to the ground. He got on the ground, he kissed that ground. He said, I will never in my life go on a boat again, you know, never in my lifetime. Well, we landed in Scotland. Got on a train the same night. Went to Ramsdon Heath, England, Ramsden Heath. Quonset hut, modern conveniences, straw mattresses, straw, made out of straw, modern. Okay. There I was. Strictly GI. You had to pull guard and everything. Went on maneuvers in Wales, which was an experience in Wales. I mean, just on maneuvers. We went on a maneuvers train again for overseas. Had everything in tip-top shape.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was unusual about maneuvers in Wales?

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: It was just like the desert in our place--rocks, lot of rocks, a lot of rocks in Wales. The people over there, I mean, we thought they talked a foreign language. A little story--I don't know what they call a store over there, wheat grocer, or whatever they call it. We went to buy bread, you know, because a soldier's always hungry. They had raisin bread. This little guy he's coming around selling us this raisin bread. Ask him how much the raisin bread costs, two far and a hay penny. Two far and a hay penny. I said what the hell is that. I gave him my money, here, take it, you know. So there I went, walked in the store. I don't know how to say, you have any bread, you know. Oh, you want bread? They were talking Gallic when I walked in, you know. I looked at them, yeah, I want bread, you know. Thought I'm in a foreign country, you know. Gallic? So anyway, we went to maneuvers over there and pulled guard duty, and this was unusual for me. On guard duty and here comes a Welshman coming up the path. Halt, who goes there? One of His Majesty's Royal Subjects. Broke me up. I said, advance and be recognized. I didn't know who the heck it was. I mean. They come up. I said, okay, pass, you know. But one of Her Majesty's Royal Subjects. Thing about England, while we were in England, we had passes. We marched in Stratford Upon Avon, Shakespeare's hometown, we marched in their parade over there. And after the parade these guys got in the middle of town shooting crap. I mean, you know. And over there a pound--what was a pound at that time? Little over two, two or three dollars. I don't know the exact exchange. These guys shooting ten pounds each. These Englishmen, that was a week's salary for them, you know, a week's salary. But they were astonished just watching the Americans play. Then you go to a pub. British soldiers couldn't afford nothing but beer, which was cheap. Americans drank up all their scotch and anything that was liquor. But anyway, we were in that small town, Ramsden Heath. Didn't, didn't amount to much. The day before--well, two weeks before invasion of France, we got notice to prepare our tanks and put up stacks for the exhaust to go up so we won't be _____ by ____ and all that. Everything cleaned off and everything ready to go. We're all set to go over. We didn't know what we were doing, what was coming, naturally, you know. All prepared. They morning of D-Day I walked outside. I looked up and, holy cow, thousands of planes, like mosquitos, in the sky. I mean, thousands of planes going over us. Right away you know it's D-Day. We hadn't hear the guns or anything, but we know it's D-Day. Thousands of planes, some pulling gliders, I mean. And told the guys, hey, this has got to be it. It was it. I mean, really. We saw General Patton in England, of course, when he drove by in his car. He was standing in salute. I mean, we may wait for him an hour to go by you in the rain, you know, wait for him to come, go by us. He didn't have us in mind. We thought we were going to be in the first wave, but it didn't work out that way. Thank God. Because I know guys who were in the first wave and it wasn't--it was sad, really sad. We lucked out. We went over there on July 21st, went overseas, but it was still harry then. We went--landed at Utah Beach on a pontoon, well, bridge, more or less, the same thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: The same thing. Going across the Channel was an experience though. That was an experience.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it rough?

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: Oh, rough. God, it was rough. I didn't get seasick, but up and down, you know. We had C Rations, the canned rations. They had a big kettle of hot water that you duck these in the hot water, to get them hot. The water'd cool off so fast you couldn't get them hot. I don't know if you ever ate greasy stew. You open a can, greasy stew. It's funny. You're hungry. You'd eat any damn thing when you're hungry. But greasy stew. Okay. Go across the--just before we got to France we got buzzed by this stupid dive bomber, you know, above us, probably run out of ammo before he got to us. Got ashore. This is France, right? I'm mean, they're not billies, I mean, cause naturally first wave, second wave, third, whatever it was, cleaned out most of the stuff for us to land. We landed. Went to ?Sainte Lo du Puits?. Remember that name because it's the first time I saw combat--somebody really blown out in combat. Went from there and went to a hedgerow. I guess just went in there to regroup or something like that, but we get in this hedgerow. The Germans had us zeroed. I mean they had us zeroed. We couldn't fire--. You dig a slit drench the size and length of your body three foot deep. And believe me, Tom, you'd never know how fast you could dig a slit trench until you're under fire. That shovel--they call it a--like--a shove that bends down like a pick. I know the name, but I can't think of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I do too, and I can't think if it.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: But you're on your stomach digging. Really. Cause you get a blast, I mean, it's shrapnel. You're digging. Boy, you're really digging. I mean, I dug my slit trench along the perimeter there and got in it. This guy in front of me, my buddy, Hergus (ph), he was driving an ammo track. He didn't dig his long enough or deep enough. Got hit in the foot right above the ankle. So he got hit. We get under fire, Captain's yelling out, somebody get that ammo track out of here. Get that ammo track. Nobody's moving. I know how to drive it, so I say, hey, get Hergus (ph) over to the Medic, you know. Somebody, goddamn, get that ammo track outside. I got in that ammo track drove it to a hedgerow gate, a gate to let cattle in about, I don't know how wide it was, 10 foot wide or something like that. Took half of the side of that thing off. Cause I didn't drive for I don't know how many months in the infantry, you know. Took that off and got that thing as far away as I could. I mean, ammo tracks were getting hit, and, see ammo flying in the air after they got hit. It's--I mean, they're duds, but I mean they're flying through the air. If you get hit by one you get killed naturally. I got the ammo track out of there. And then after that I was assigned to this track at nighttime. They never drove an ammo track at nighttime with a slit in the windshield. A slit?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: All you had a florescent circle or track in front of you. If you're used to driving those things, I mean, oh, man, they could go up and down hills. We were going toward Brest, which I didn't know at the time. I'll show you some maps, you tell me where you're at. I mean, you don't know where you're at. So many towns.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: I drove all that night. We're on a march. We pull up in daytime. We pull off to the side of the road, I mean, you know, to refuel and all that. I don't know who drove after I got out. I got out, thank God, you know. Because you're going up and all of a sudden you see a florescent button, you stop. You have to stop when you hit the thing, the ammo in front of you, you hit one of those ammo trailers. So going up in Brest. Course, we encountered light resistence, light. First experience in combat was we were in the fire position, and here comes a Cossack on a horse, with his sword drawn, that's going to attack tanks. Must have had some guys in the back of him, cause we didn't see those guys in back of him. He's over there going to charge like, you know, like The Charge of the Light Brigade. With a sword. I looked at the Captain, Captain, what do you think? He says, no, let him go. He thought he was going to attack our tank. I said, oh, no, you know. I mean, he was in uniform too, I mean. Looked good, I mean, with sword drawn. What the hell, you know. But we let him go.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I thought Cossacks were Russian.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: I don't know who he was. I don't know who the hell he was. He might have been Mongolian or some other--.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Somebody pressed into service with the German army though, right? I guess.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: I mean, with the sword--we only saw one guy though. I thought we'd see a bunch of guys behind with tanks ready to, you know, open up. Captain looked, we looked. Okay, let him go, you know. He took off. But our Captain at the time, Captain Graham, for some reason he went out on recon. He was in artillery. He shouldn't have gone on recon. He went out on recon. Didn't know the password. We had a password every night, different password. We pulled guard, pulled guard, every night in combat, every night. He didn't know the password coming back, and he got hit three times by our own men because he didn't know the password. Dark you can't tell uniforms, you know. Sometimes Germans had American uniforms, so you couldn't trust nobody coming in. Got hit three times. Nothing fatal though. Wounds, but nothing fatal. Another initiation into combat, three of the infantry guys were up front, you know. They saw about four German soldiers with their hands up, you know, in the field. Souvenir time, you know, right away they think souvenir time. They went out to get these souvenirs off these German solders, right? Before they hit the German solders they dropped the machine guns down, mowed the three guys down, killed them. I mean for souvenirs. So they had an ambulance to take these guys out of there. Nobody come out of that--. I mean, we opened up on those guys. Nobody come out of there alive. This one small stinking town I remember it, Armacourt. And that was one town everybody I talked to might think badly-- remember this one little town, Armacourt. It changed hands five times. This was really the first big initiation in combat. Changed hands five times. Truck load of GI's come out of there stacked like cord wood on six-by-sixes, and Germans the same way, come out there truck loads of them. This little stupid town, it wasn't worth one American soldier. We had these reunions and the first thing they'd think about Armacourt, because we'd had such a horrible time in there. I mean, you know. The Germans had the high ground. We'd try and get the high ground off of them, why I don't know. But that town wasn't worth one GI. After we got done with it it wasn't worth nothing to anybody anyway, not even France. But we're going to Brest, right? Small resistence. We pull off the side of the road one time. I mean, we're setting up machine guns and all that. Here comes a German personnel carrier. We're setting up our guns and, whee, he passes us by with five or six guys in a personnel carrier. Couldn't fire cause we weren't set up. They didn't know we were there. I don't think they knew we were there. They passed by us like a bat out of hell, and we couldn't fire at them too fast. But in artillery's it's different. Like when we were in firing position I'm ______+, right? Infantry needs protection. Need somebody on telephone to call back coordinates and all that. When we call back coordinates I was 21--20A, call 21. No, 21B, call 21 which was our Captain. Called back coordinates to him. He'd either take me to exe track to get the fire emission going or he'd do it himself. But I was on BC track all the way through, BC track, a track with radio and all that. 21, 21A. No, 21B, not 21A.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: BC track?

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: BC, battery commanders.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: Battery commanders track. There was six of us guys in there. Three go up front, and when we were up front, the three'd have to pull extra guard duty at nighttime. Everybody had guard duty, everybody. There was no rank in our outfit. Everybody thinks tanks they're easy, you know, compared to infantry, and maybe they are, but you ever load tanks with gas, 100 gallons of gas, and shells? You ever fire--nobody thinks that firing you have to get your supplies in there. I mean, there's no rank. We all worked. Want to hear about the Army, I mean, we got trained for combat, you have all buddies. You see solders yelling at people in movies, whoa, whoa, whoa, yelling, they're not in combat. Cause you know, hey, he got shot, you know. Nobody yells in combat. Nobody has stripes on in combat. Nobody has bars on in combat. Be a perfect target. You know. But anyway we're going to Brest and get to Brest. Three combat commands. I was in Combat Command B, our outfit. It was A, B, and C. Going to attack Brest. We're up in the hills. ____+ attacked after 1200 hours. Up in the hills smoking, and I looked at the guys. We always had this saying, we'd be home for Christmas. Said, we won't be home for Christmas if you we go in there. It was a seaport, right, defended by Germans. And we got the wrong G2 on that place. They said it wasn't well fortified. But they didn't know that other troops come in to support the outfit that was in there. So just about ready to attack the right G2 come out, and they called off the attack. We just held there, right, till the infantry come up. I don't know how many divisions it took to take that little port. It was one of the last ports taken. We were going in there--there's a monument there with a cross over it. But anyway we held there till the infantry come relieve us and then we were on the march again. I drew up my statistics. 242 days, constant combat. We're always in contact with the enemy. Always in contact. We go up to a certain point, hit a hot spot. Standard fire, ____+ fire on them, and we wait till the infantry come up to take over, you know, clean out the town. Then we go around it, attack again. I don't know how many different, oh, different outfits we were loaned to to combat command. They want to experiment a little, they sent us over there. I mean, Patton didn't care. He had two orders. You go till you run out of gas or ammo. That's all he give us, orders. The guy never came around--like the Seventh Army you had to be shaven, tie on and everything--never done that. Never had to shave, no tie. Gave us orders--we got compliments from going 200 miles in 13 days, I think, with tanks. I mean, through combat zone, Combat Command B. Every combat command has a different story, cause we'd attack one place, A, well, there was always one in reserve. Like, you'd attack, B attack, and C would be a reserve. Then you reverse. I mean, you know, you'd be a reserve in case somebody got knocked out bad, you know, you'd replace them. We went through, I don't know, I'd have to go through the sequence in a book to tell you where we went from there, but 3,200 miles of combat, 3,200 miles. Dead people. I don't know if anybody smelled the dead flesh. But horses, they had horse drawn vehicles, and down the road if your track hit fire or anything the gas smelled, oh my God. But dead people, displaced people, moving--you felt sorry for people. But, hey, you had to do your job. Firing at people. One day I fired somebody .50 caliber rounds, I mean, had to show them my track. I mean--. But that was what they train you for. Guy when I was in basic training gave us good advice. He'd come from Africa while we were in basic training. He come in to talk to us while we were in instruction. He looked at us, said, you know, don't be a dumb son of a B. If you go overseas in combat, any maneuvers, if you don't kill those guys they're going to kill your rear end, right? So it has stuck with me too. I mean, it stuck with me. I'm German, and going over in Germany. I mean, you know, I could talk a little bit. I couldn't talk real fluent, but I could talk a little bit. But anyway, that stuck with me. And the training these guys gave us from Anapolis, I mean, they really worked us. I mean, every morning five-mile jog, every morning, and full field, attack. And time I was ready it come back to me, all that stuck with me. Maybe that's why I didn't get hit. I was cautious always. And if there were snipers in the area, naturally your infantry takes six guys and clear the area, you know. Go out. Fine, if we do, fine, they won't come back. But, I mean, anything--you're a rookie, you're a new man, infantry training, going on artillery, so I went up forward. I mean, always protect these lieutenants and call back coordinates to them. Anyway over a period of time you see--. We were with the infantry. The guys I trained with they were our infantry, 50th and Ninth Infantry. I go up and went to the USO, say, hey, you so-in-so, you know, talk to him, how you doing? As you go along they start dropping out. Where's so-in-so? He bought it. Oh, he's in hospital. I mean, you see less and less of these guys, infantry. I thank God I wasn't in the infantry. Thank God. I mean, the artillery just was a class outfit, crack troops, class. They knew what they were doing, and they were good. They were very good. We went up to Nance, France. That's where I wrote my wife. My wife, you know, I write to her--you can't tell her where we're at. So I wrote her a letter. I said, Dorothy, how's your--she wanted to know where I was at--how's your Aunt Nancy. I know she had an Aunt Pauline and all that. I said how is your Aunt Nancy? She never got the thing. She wrote back, I don't have an Aunt Nancy. I tried to tell her where I was at. But we were in Orleans, France. We captured a German supply, liquor supply, depot, right? We were issued a quart of wine, cognac, rum--what's the other--wine, cognac, rum. We got champagne in a basement some place. But we always had booze in our track. We had filled a box, you know, in the back of our track, the BC track, for booze and all that. So we always had a supply of booze. But you weren't allowed to drink, naturally. Well, we bypassed that. One time we went up front for three days. And it was tough up there, and we come back on a rainy day. What the hell, you know, we put up a piece of canvass next to our track, six of us guys got together underneath there, cause we just come off the line, and drank them, everybody brought a bottle. We're drinking and all of a sudden get called. We got to go up front for a relay station for another outfit that was too far away to pass back their fire information. You can fire a gun seven miles, you know. So we're all half bombed. Get in the truck, go up to where we made contact with the other radio operators and relay the message back. And we're all half bombed in the middle of the field. All of sudden, whee, we hear a whistle. We're cooking our meal, right, over a little gas stove we had. Whee, short. Well, we're artillery, you know, one long, one short, next one's going to drop here. Well, what dropped in was a dud. I looked at the Sargent, I said, hey Studley, (ph) he's out to get our rear ends, you know. Let's get the heck out of here. So we moved back in a orchard, a little orchard, over there where we could relay this thing. We were half bombed, but we could relay it and we could talk. But at night we pulled guard duty. Every night you had guard duty. Pulled guard duty. I'm on guard duty. A big one of the guys was up in a rig. Along comes a guy down the road. We heard him, I mean, you know. Halt, who goes there? Comrade, comrade, he said. Three o'clock and we ain't got no comrade. Opens up a .50 caliber, you know. I don't know what happened to him. Anyway, that was the last time we drank that much, cause we--you know, tension, you have to relieve. But we killed some bottles. One time--. Anyway. We're going along. We went to Nance-- Orleans, we got booze. Nance, France we fought over there. Went up to a bunch of small towns. I can't tell you the names. But anyway, we were _____+ coming up to the Bulge. Course, we had a lot of places in between there. I don't remember the names of the small towns. We never--we never were in a house all during combat. We were always in contact with the enemy. We were always dug in outside. Rain, shine, whatever. Ever dig a slit trench and put a little tent over it, I mean, you know, tent over it? Wake up in the mornings and it's full of water. Dump the water, you know, dump the rain and get all wet from the water. Which ain't bad, but in the wintertime, snow, ain't too good, cause you wake up real fast. You never take your boots off. You always have your gun on your side in that little slit trench, always. When you do take your boots off--I used my boots for a pillow. Put the heels outside, with leather inside. Course, my bedroll, I mean--course, we were lucky we had bedrolls cause we were in tanks, you know, we could store our bedrolls. But you never take your clothes off in combat. We're leading up to Bastogne to the ____+ mines, and we're in the holding position over there. Naturally, when you're in the holding position you go forward three days and come back for three days. Get fire, harassing fire. You're on guard duty, Have to go up on tank for harassing fire. You load up so many rounds of ammo to replace what you've fired. You fire, have the guns set up. Harassing fire at crossroads or something. You have intermittent firing. So you do that, you fire, I mean, fire. I was firing over there pulling a ____ way up on a hill, some German was firing at something. I don't know what he was firing at, but he ain't firing on me. Thank God. Hey, don't spot me, please, don't spot me. Anyway, ____+. It's getting cold. I mean, December. It wasn't as cold as where we were going, but, anyway, got the order to go on to Bastogne. Where the hell's Bastogne, you know. We have no Bastogne, man. And get orders to pull out. Night march. I'm driving the Captain in the Jeep. Going down the road, no lights. Can't have no lights. We're ahead of the battalion. Had to pull in to get positions for our tanks to pull in off the road, cause we couldn't make Bastogne that night. We're going along 50, well, about 50 mile an hour, top speed. All to guide me was a row of trees on the road, I mean, you know. Dark as heck. Go along 55 miles an hour. Pull off. He said, he knew-- you knew just how far a tank could go without refueling--so pull off here. We pull off next to a barn. This was Christmas Eve day. Pull in this place. Got our guns in firing position, but we weren't firing, cause we weren't close enough to Bastogne naturally. But I had to pull guard duty that Christmas Eve up this road, protect the tanks and tracks. Had two men on guard duty, one forward and one back. In case you got knocked out this guy's going to knock off the guy got you, you know. They go back to reverse. Three hours in crunchy snow. But we had a barn with straw in it that we were in. We slept in that in the straw. We sang Christmas carols in the barn with straw in it. Next morning, eight, on our way to Bastogne. Where's Bastogne, where's Bastogne? What Bastogne? Battle of the Bulge, right? We didn't know that. We get in there. The Fourth Army's in there before us, our sister outfit. They took a beating going in. So we go to Bastogne gung-ho, right? I mean Bastogne. We see Germans in the woods, camouflaged. White tanks. You could see them through binoculars. So we're green. Our tanks, they're in camouflage. Get a firing position. Fire at them. We hit the woods pretty good with our fire. But they're firing at us, so we had to get out of there. We're in the middle of Bastogne, I mean, and had direct fire on this BC track. Some shrapnel hit our radiator, but it didn't do much damage, just a small leak. We had that fixed when we got back to camp. But we're in the middle of Bastogne. I was talking to some of these 101st Airborne. They told me, you know, said, we held this place. We had guys hit three times. I mean, and as long as they could move they had to carry a gun, really. This was a man from the 101st Airborne telling me this. Well, naturally we took a pounding too. Some of our guys got killed. This lieutenant I used to go up forward with, talk about families and all that. He had a year-old kid when he left for the Army, and he told me about his kid and all that. While were up forward, naturally, we had time to talk. And he was up on a tank. He should know better than to drive a tank up in a forward position on it. He got half his head blown off, I mean, you know. Se we're back in battery, and we were going to go get his body. Captain give us direct orders not to go up there. Go up there you'd be Court-Martialed, you know. So it's a good thing we didn't do it, cause if we'd went up there we'd probably got killed. But anyway, snow, cold, nobody ever realizes not till you go out there and take a leak going down in the snow. Snow was that high really. Cold. Had to go to the john, right? What you do you have that entrenching tool, entrenching tool. Dug a hole where you could go. I mean, didn't go too long really. I mean, to dig in the snow, you hit this entrenching tool like a pick, I mean, get one lump out as you go to dig in. Me and another guy dug in the side of a mule trail, well, cow trail or horse trail. We had it a shelter half over it. It's nice and cozy. We got some straw, you know, and put in there. It's cozy in there. But pulled guard duty that night. We're all covered in snow. Nobody knew where in the hell we were at, so we had watches we passed out from one thing to another. So somebody's calling my name. I said, oh, my God. It's warm, you know, you're enclosed. You're warm in there and got to go out in the cold pull guard, have guard, duty. _____+, what the hell. So anyway, fire position in Bastogne, I mean, firing--____ was in there at the time. They had kids, 15, and old men 65. I don't know how old they were, just seemed dead on the street. Dead horses, dead things. Death, nothing but death. We were there till January. Our tour was nowhere. We had to go where our combat commanded. Didn't say get in a house and stay out of it, you know. We had to go out and went on the Autobahn. We're were going to Frankfurt am Main. We were going to attack Frankfurt am Main. So got on the Autobahn, pull off to the side road and pull in a field. The Germans must have had this place surrounded. They had a church, they had ammo in a church, you know. If they got caught, it's their fault, no pity, you know, cause they directed fire. And if I got caught, no pity, you know. Anyway, directed fire on us. We saw them in the church, so blow up the top of the church, naturally. Get on the Autobahn, go to attack Frankfurt am Main. In the middle of town--the Germans had the upper ground in Frankfurt am Main. There's a nurse in the middle of the street. I'm watching this nurse. We're in the middle of the town doing the combat thing, convoy. She's moving. I thought she's helping, you know, somebody wounded. I look out the cab, I said, she's directing fire on our rear end, you know. Well, naturally, used better terms than that. Got her out of there. She's directing the fire on us. White uniform, they're up in the hill. Once we got her out of there we were in good shape. Cause, I mean, we spotted a gun and started firing, you know. But she directed fire on us. Okay. Go take Frankfurt am Main. We go up to the next town. There were so many towns we took and fought in, I mean, I forget half of them. We can't remember all of them. But, anyway, we go up to--had light resistance up to Miramar, Miramar. Go up to, I think it's the Elbe River past ?Miramar?. We come back and the Captain give us a good decision. We had to wait till the Russians went over--well, the 29th Infantry, went to meet the Russians. Anyway, he gave us a decision to make. Look, you could go in German barracks, be GI, or we can camp out here. We've got tents. END OF SIDE ONE

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was your job most of the time?

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: No, it was half and half. Go with the group. Two in back and two in front. We're on holding position in the woods, you know, going forward. There was two groups, half and half, I mean, go forward and then come back for the battery. You know, you're on radio or on the thing, telephone. Sometimes we had strung telephone lines. But we're in the holding position now, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: But being attacked, you know, up forward, I mean, you're always moving. But you observe the enemy. Watch for any little detail. There was one really smart--commando tanks. We were up on military ridge. Military ridge is half way up the hill, right? We watch--sometimes the entire infantry, you know, watching for anything we can fire at. We spot four tanks coming down this road up on a hill. So we fired, called fire emission. One over, which is naturel, one over, cause can't get the distance. Then the next one has smoke going over, right? And then one short. This guy in the tank, he had smoke on his tank. All these tanks released their smoke. He must have got where we release the smoke. Couldn't see nothing. I mean, we couldn't fire at the guy because we couldn't spot them. The tank, I mean, took off. We never got that guy. He was a really smart guy. But when you're observing you can see--like where I nearly got it. I mean, you can't get too cocky until the end of the war, I mean. You stand up looking, you know. _____+ covered by a tree. Boop, boop. Infantry training. Flat on my rear covered, I mean, flat. Some guy spotted me and I didn't spot him. But they were in a bunch of woods and we were driving forward. They come out of those woods and caught fire emission. And another time we're up forward and here comes a bunch of Nazi's, goose-stepping down the road. We're in combat. Parade. They're in parade uniform and everything. Not for long they weren't. But fire emission on them. Anyway, up to Miramar, patrol seven towns, patrol them, you know, keep the place in order. Occupation troops after the war. This is after the war. And had to patrol seven towns. Before we hit Bastogne we were--no, this is after Bastogne. This is in Germany. Germany we told these people, surrender your town. Put white sheets, anything white, out, we won't bother you. You put white sheets out. This one day several little villages, no white sheets. Orders, fire at anything, anybody. Go through town. That evening seven burgs--we're up on a hill- -seven burgs were burning, because they didn't put the white sheets out. Another group we were going into town, and how come the town's empty, nobody's there. Unusual, unusual. So had guns naturally, always had guns. But go up to a little dried out river bed or creek, whatever it was. Go have a look around, all of a sudden a row of people in there. Look at them. I say, hey, go back home. I mean, they ain't no soldiers. We're looking for soldiers, naturally. But naturally they change to civilian clothes, and I couldn't tell. But anyway, come on back, we ain't going to kill you people. You should have put a towel out, a white flag, anything out, you know. Go on home, I told them, go on home. They looked at me, yeah, go on home. Then patrolling around our compound, we had German people come evacuate the houses. German people talking German. I couldn't understand their talk, you know. And here was this one girl saying that she was raped by some infantry guy, you know, and all of a sudden my face must have changed expression. And right away they clammed up, because it was just like they were controlled by the government. If somebody knew too much, boom. Anyway, we went in this camp, this tent city, where we stayed till we were told to mover out. Till we add up our points after the war. We had patrols, five or six towns there occupied. Got to know the people, I mean, you know, and they were fairly good to us. And we got beer from Miramar. ?Miramar? beer was supposed to be good. We had 55 gallons always in the tent city, you know. It was always warm. Warm beer, is warm beer. And they also had German schnapps. This is after the war now, I mean, you know. Had to pull guard duty then too. Patrol these towns in Jeeps and with a .30-caliber machine gun. But anyway, got German schnapps, and this stuff, I put a little in my canteen, my canteen. I'm writing my wife a letter from my bunk and I'm drinking that stuff. Hey, it tasted really good. That was about six or six-thirty in the evening. Woke up the next morning, I mean, pad on my chest, pen on the floor, no, no, this stuff hit me. No hang-over or nothing, but it hit me. Anyway we patrolled towns. Then we were called back and had to move out back to Frankfurt, because the Germans were going to take over East Germany and we took over Miramar. Go back to Frankfurt. We were on the Fourth of July. We had to patrol there too, patrol bridges, watch bridges, every evening so nobody'd blow them up. Back to Frankfurt, Fourth of July, getting our guns, we fired. All these Germans running and diving, you know. The Fourth of July. They didn't know no better. But after that I got my points, my summons, my 85th point. Got out on points. Had to leave my outfit go to 28th Infantry to come back home, 28th Infantry. We were scheduled to go over to fight the Japanese. So naturally, go back on a cattle car to Camp Philip Morris in France, to ship back home with the 28th Infantry. And naturally you're anxious to get back home, but, you know you've going to get reassigned, I mean. And luckily enough the Jap war was over, the atom bomb. So I come back to the States, I mean, it's something special. I mean, they had us quarantined. In New Jersey we got quarantined. Camp--what was the name of the camp?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Kilmer?

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: Kilmer, yeah. Went back there. But the day Japanese surrendered we were allowed in town. We were allowed--. We were in the barracks, I mean, quarantined. But we were on our way home for furlough, we thought, then get shipped out to fight the Japanese. But the war was over. And I come home, I mean. We come home on the Marshall Joffre, a French boat, a crummy boat. But anyway, we were on a promenade deck in August, which was beautiful. I mean, you know, beautiful calm weather on that promenade deck waiting with our bedrolls on the deck. Just like a cruise, I mean, compared to the one we went over there on. Bump, bump, I mean, big waves, side waves. But coming home, I mean, something special about it. Got to the Statute of Liberty had a little tug boat come out play songs for us. The funniest part of it was one of the guys from the Battle of the Bulge, Art Began (ph), he was on the boat coming home, and he was with the Glenn Miller Band. He was practicing always on the boat, always. So when this tug boat come out to play, serenade them, when they come in, the Glenn Miller Band come up and serenaded the tug boat. The guy told that story so many times. The guy's dead now. But one hell of a guy, Art Began (ph). You want to go in detail about combat. You don't want that, do you?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, whatever you'd like to tell me, sure. I mean, it's up to you whatever you want to share.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: Too many stories. I mean, fire--.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You mentioned about the Lieutenant. Did you want to mention any other buddies?

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: Yeah, I mean, guys in my outfit. Well, we lost some guys with counter fire with mortar, and we lost guys--dead, I mean, but--or shooting at people, you know. I ain't never fired a gun no more. Never have. Fired too many. And at that age, you're 22, I mean, 23 years old, you don't realize what you're doing. I mean, you know. Cause you're fighting for your country. They tell you to fight for your family and all that. So it's your obligation to do it, and you do it. But to see people's bodies and soldiers bodies and all that. You lucked out. I lucked out. I feel lucky, real lucky, to live this long. My wife says how come you can remember all that. Well, it's something you can't forget. You can not forget. Anyway.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories about your first day in combat?

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: The first day in combat was getting off that pontoon bridge. The first day in combat scared me, naturally. You didn't know what to expect. But you're always busy. You're always doing something. You have to get in gun a position, and we went to Saint Lo, we were ready to take it, but Saint Lo had been taken already. Like I said, first day in combat, was when the Captain taken three bullet holes in him, you know. Then we fired on this stupid ambulance. But after a while you get hard. You don't want to remember anything anymore. You don't want to remember anything anymore. But maybe it's better; I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you and your buddies do anything to relieve the tension while you were there?

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: Drink. Yeah, drink. That relieved the tension. I know, one time I come close, I mean, really buying it. I had dug a slit trench in front of this track, my buddy's track. He dug his slit trench in front of his track, and I dug it next to--a little further down, about ten yards down. And we're talking, all of a sudden we encounter fire. And I dove in his thing cause it's closer. When you encounter shrapnel--when you're in the slit trench the shrapnel goes up and out. And if you're in the slit trench chances are you won't get hit. He wasn't there so I dug in his, dove in his. One landed right on mine. One landed right on mine. Dirt on me. If I was in that thing--been cannon fodder. But anyway, there's so many different--. See, every day in combat--well, every day you ain't firing a gun. Most days, every day. We're firing guns at planes. We were on a road watching these German planes _______--three planes _______ in a column other side of a hill. We're watching these guys _____, go down ______, right? So these other columns firing at them. They come on us. We knocked two or three planes. As they come over the hill, we got them, you know. Now, I'm sure I got one of them, cause they tell you always fire in front of a guy and let him run into you, you know. We knocked out two or three planes. We saw them go down, poof, you know, crash. Then we're in a column and a German plane comes over us, but had orders not to fire, because we fired the thing would explode and hit all our troops on the column. Another time, the Captain says, stay with your vehicles, you know, had planes come down ______, ____+ drove in ditches, you know. Another time we were in a firing position and the planes that come over ______ and here comes a big object floating down right in our area. I look, oh, jeez, you know, a bomb. It is big. Airplane dropped his extra gas tank. It fell in our area. If it would have been a bomb, oh--. And same thing. You see the guys that get battle fatigue. I don't know if you ever know what battle fatigue is. The guy just--just like Alzheimer's, they say it's just--more or less just ______+ shaking and all that. Another guy ______ stayed on _______ he got it. I mean. Well, all I can say, the infantry training I had was the best thing I had. But not being in combat and infantry is, cause that's the worst place to be, believe me, worst place. I saw some of these guys, my buddies, I mean, guys I trained with. This one guy, saw him up there. He was with the 50th Infantry. Hey, Al, how you doing. I said where were you the last time I was there. He say, they sent me back; they say I'm nuts. The guy's crazy as hell. I'm talking to him. He's crazy. I knew him before. Oh, Jesus, you know. They sent him back on the front lines. Batty. Anyway, like I say, I looked at lot of stuff. I mean, I can't go 3,200 hundred miles in combat and tell you every city we went to. Some of these guys could tell me what city he lived in, I mean, was in, and all that. I can't do it, because I was never in a city that long.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's pretty weird for them to remember all that. From the people that I've talked to they don't usually remember the names of the towns.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: I'll show you some. You tell if you can remember the name of all these towns. I mean, here's the map that went to. 3,200 miles of combat, and I can't remember the names of these towns.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, exactly. Oh, my, big map.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: Those are all the outfits we fought for and with.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Who were you attached with? Which division were you attached with?

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: Sixth Armored Division, Third Army, Patton's Army. Third Army. Go all the way through there. How many towns can you remember. The big ones you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, exactly.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: All these outfits were attack or support. All of these outfits. The 212's.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: Combat Command B was one of the best ones in that. Course, you know, this map is old.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah, exactly. When you think about that experience over there, does any one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: Well, that Amacourt, that little town that we lost so many people in, Amacourt, France. I mean, we were new in combat then too, I mean, you know, fairly new in combat. ______+. And that was a little stinking town.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: But after we took the town, it's funny, experience, I mean. Patrolling the town after we took it there was a guy urinating against the building, woman walks by and started talking to him. Unheard in our society. Starts talking to him, he's urinating and she starts talking to him. But little town, we blew it all to hell. And you see all those dead bodies for a little town. It wasn't worth it, really wasn't worth it. But, I mean, had to take it, they get orders, you know. You know, everybody can remember exact orders that they got. We just had two orders, attack. Attack, attack, attack. One time they were going too fast they had to stop us. I mean. One time we cut off three days, I mean.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: Cut off three days and we ate cheese, the dinner supply, for three days. We ate all the good stuff before then. We were cut of for three days. Like I say, every day was different. I mean, a lot of days it's easy going; I mean, you know, no problem. But get tough days, I mean, like to forget them. A weird thing, check our ammo and all that. Going into areas you have to check all the stuff you need to have them bring up to you. I know, I drove this Captain, he didn't like me. He was from the South; I was from up North. I'm driving down the road to Bastogne, snow covered, about three foot of snow. I asked him one question. Captain--he had to go to a meeting, right? Where the hell is the road. I can't see the road. There's woods and then there's a field, like a farm field. I'm going along all of a sudden I get in the ditch. Jeep got four-wheel drive, back up, go about another 100 yards and, pow, I don't know where the road's at. There's no poles. There's no distance points to point us, you know. Let me drive, Al. Get in. Please. He gets in, he goes about 10 yards, he's in the ditch. All of a sudden it dawned on me, there's no road. How you going to drive. So I got back in. I had to laugh. Well, the guy, we just didn't click, because his name was Captain Lee. I don't know if he was from the regular Lee family or what. But I was from the North; he was from the South. Anyway, I get in; I get smart. There's a road--trees, there's woods, maybe there's a road, if I stay to the left more, maybe--. That's what I done. I got him to his meeting. But I don't know, picking our positions _____+ come up to go forward naturally. Always forward. Go down a cow path, thing's at a, I don't know, a 90-degree angle, I'm on this side driving with one hand hanging on so I don't fall over on him. He's over there. He tells me go over there. I said, look, I'm thinking to myself, if this Jeep goes over I'm bailing out this way. He's on that side, bye.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Albert Pekrul
sp.p: But anyway, and traveling forward, I'm going forward. See a Jeep hit a land mine, it's up in a tree, I mean. So many experiences, I mean, you know. You can't put all those experiences down, whatever it is. I mean, it's impossible. Cause, everything is different. You get souvenirs, I mean. This one kid I called Squeaky Taylor. He got a souvenir. I don't know why he shot himself through the hand. I mean what the hell. Another guy got his souvenir ____. I said, get that guy away from me. He's got it pointed at me. I said, hey, get that damn gun away from me. But this Squeaky Taylor I met him at a reunion. He was a real skinny Texan kid. I met him about six, seven years ago at a reunion of the Sixth Armored Division. The first one I came to, right? So they told me, his name was G. W. Taylor, said G. W. Taylor's in the reunion. I said G. W., nee Squeaky? Yeah. So where's he at? I go up to him. Big, huge guy. He's an ex-deputy sheriff. How the hell are you, Squeaky? He slapped my back; I hugged the guy. His son's standing there. His son's breaking up, you know. He was a thin Texan kid, I mean, real thin. Here he's a big fellow now. Oh, God. Said, Al, you know, we couldn't do this in combat, you know. I mean, he was something else. But anyway, lot of memories, you know. You just you can't tell them all. Combat, dead people, killing. My son has a firing range. I don't want to fire a gun. I got guns I haven't fired. I know what they can do. I mean, and it ain't funny. Like these movies, I mean, kids--there's too much gunfire in movies. I mean, it's ridiculous. To go and see what it does to people, ain't funny. Like I say, I got drafted. I was in Three C Camp. The day I got on the train I come in ______+ because of the training in Three C Camp. I don't know. I'm the kind of guy won't have anybody do anything I won't do, you know. And combat, too many stories, I mean, you know. So, I don't want it. Anyway, my story.
